qkv.d:
Queries, keys and values are three learned linear projections of the same token representations that let attention decide which tokens to read from and what to read. Each token's query expresses what it is looking for, each key expresses what that token offers for matching, and each value carries the content that is actually passed along. The dot product of a query with every key gives a relevance score; a softmax turns the scores into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of the values.

Separating matching (Q·K) from content (V) is what makes attention flexible: two tokens can be highly relevant to each other while contributing information unrelated to the features used for matching. W_Q, W_K and W_V are ordinary learned weight matrices. Keys and values need not come from a different source than queries: in self-attention all three come from the same sequence, and only cross-attention draws keys and values from a different one.
qkv.f: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V,  Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
B, T, d = 2, 5, 16
x = torch.randn(B, T, d)              # token representations

W_q = nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)     # what each token looks for
W_k = nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)     # what each token offers for matching
W_v = nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)     # the content each token passes on

Q, K, V = W_q(x), W_k(x), W_v(x)
scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / d ** 0.5   # (B, T, T) relevance
weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)           # each row sums to 1
out = weights @ V                             # weighted sum of values
print(out.shape, weights[0, 0].sum().item())

mha.d:
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel on lower-dimensional projections of the input and concatenates their results. The model dimension d_model is split into h heads of size d_model/h; each head has its own query, key and value projections, computes scaled dot-product attention independently, and the concatenated outputs pass through a final linear projection W_O.

Because each head works in its own subspace, different heads can specialize: some track syntactic dependencies, some attend to the previous token, others copy rare names from far away. The total compute is about the same as a single full-width head, since each head is narrower. Multiple heads are therefore a way to get several attention patterns per layer at no extra cost. A frequent misunderstanding is that every head learns a distinct, interpretable role; in practice many heads are redundant, and studies have shown that a sizable fraction can be pruned after training with little loss in accuracy.
mha.f: MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head₁,…,head_h)·W_O,  headᵢ = Attention(QWᵢ_Q, KWᵢ_K, VWᵢ_V)

Capturing several dependency types per layer

import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
B, T, d_model, n_heads = 2, 10, 64, 8
x = torch.randn(B, T, d_model)

mha = nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=d_model, num_heads=n_heads,
                            batch_first=True)
# Self-attention: query, key and value are the same sequence
out, attn = mha(x, x, x, average_attn_weights=False)
print(out.shape)    # (2, 10, 64)
print(attn.shape)   # (2, 8, 10, 10): one T x T map per head

crossattn.d:
Cross-attention is attention in which the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values come from another, letting one stream read information from a second source. In an encoder-decoder Transformer, each decoder layer projects its own hidden states into queries and attends over keys and values projected from the encoder output, so every generated token can look at the whole input.

The same mechanism conditions generation on other modalities. Text-to-image diffusion models use cross-attention so that image latents (queries) attend to text-encoder embeddings (keys and values), and some vision-language models insert cross-attention layers so text tokens can attend to image features. The output length always matches the query sequence, while the key and value sequence can have any length. One practical limitation is cost: the score matrix is query length times source length, so very long source contexts, such as many retrieved documents, make each cross-attention layer expensive in memory and compute.
crossattn.f: CrossAttn(X_q, X_kv) = softmax((X_q W_Q)(X_kv W_K)ᵀ/√d_k)·(X_kv W_V)

Conditioning diffusion image generation on text prompts
Speech recognition decoders reading audio features

Because the text embedding is fixed for a request, its keys and values can be computed once and reused across all denoising steps to reduce latency.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
d_model, n_heads = 64, 4
decoder_states = torch.randn(2, 7, d_model)   # target side: 7 tokens
encoder_output = torch.randn(2, 20, d_model)  # source side: 20 tokens

cross_attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(d_model, n_heads, batch_first=True)
# Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder
out, weights = cross_attn(query=decoder_states,
                          key=encoder_output,
                          value=encoder_output)
print(out.shape)      # (2, 7, 64): length follows the queries
print(weights.shape)  # (2, 7, 20): each target token over all source tokens

causalmask.d:
A causal mask prevents each position in a sequence from attending to positions that come after it, so a model's prediction for token t depends only on tokens 1 to t. It is implemented by adding negative infinity to the attention scores above the diagonal of the T×T score matrix before the softmax, which sets those attention weights to exactly zero.

The mask is what makes parallel training of autoregressive models possible. With it, a decoder-only model processes an entire sequence in one forward pass and computes the next-token loss at every position simultaneously, without any position seeing the token it must predict. At inference the same rule holds naturally, because future tokens do not exist yet. A common mistake when writing custom attention is to combine the causal mask incorrectly with a padding mask, or to use a large finite negative number in low precision, where it can overflow or fail to zero out the weights.
causalmask.f: Mᵢⱼ = 0 if j ≤ i, −∞ if j > i;  A = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k + M)
u: Training GPT-style decoder-only language models
Autoregressive decoders in encoder-decoder models
Preventing future leakage in sequence forecasting
causalmask.x: A team pretraining a code completion model packs many files into fixed-length sequences and applies a causal mask so every position is trained to predict the next token in parallel. They also add document boundaries to the mask so tokens from one file cannot attend to an unrelated file packed before it.
causalmask.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
B, h, T, d = 1, 2, 5, 8
q, k, v = (torch.randn(B, h, T, d) for _ in range(3))

# Upper-triangular entries (future positions) get -inf
mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / d ** 0.5
scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
out = weights @ v
print(weights[0, 0])   # lower-triangular attention pattern

# Equivalent fused call
out2 = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
print(torch.allclose(out, out2, atol=1e-5))

posenc.d:
Positional encoding injects information about token order into a Transformer, which would otherwise treat its input as an unordered set because attention is permutation-equivariant. The original Transformer adds a fixed sinusoidal vector to each token embedding: each pair of dimensions is a sine and cosine at a different frequency, ranging from fast oscillations to very slow ones, so every position gets a unique pattern.

A useful property of sinusoids is that the encoding of position p + k is a linear function (a rotation) of the encoding of position p, which makes relative offsets easy for the model to use. Many models such as BERT and GPT-2 instead learn an absolute position embedding table. Learned tables cannot represent positions beyond the maximum length seen in training, and sinusoidal encodings also extrapolate poorly in practice. This limitation is one reason modern LLMs moved to relative schemes such as RoPE and ALiBi.
u: Adding order information to Transformer inputs
Encoding timesteps in diffusion models
Representing patch positions in Vision Transformers
posenc.x: An image generation team encodes the diffusion timestep with a sinusoidal embedding followed by a small MLP, the same construction used for token positions. Because the function is fixed and smooth, the model can be sampled with step schedules different from the ones used in training.
posenc.c:
import numpy as np

def sinusoidal_encoding(max_len, d_model):
    pos = np.arange(max_len)[:, None]                 # (max_len, 1)
    i = np.arange(0, d_model, 2)[None, :]             # even dimension indices
    freq = 1.0 / (10000 ** (i / d_model))             # geometric frequencies
    pe = np.zeros((max_len, d_model))
    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(pos * freq)                  # even dims: sine
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(pos * freq)                  # odd dims: cosine
    return pe

pe = sinusoidal_encoding(max_len=128, d_model=64)
token_emb = np.random.randn(10, 64)
x = token_emb + pe[:10]                               # added, not concatenated
print(x.shape, pe[0, :4], pe[1, :4])

rope.d:
Rotary Position Embedding encodes position by rotating query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position, so that their dot product depends only on the relative distance between tokens. Each pair of dimensions in a query or key is treated as a 2D point and rotated by p·θᵢ, where p is the position and θᵢ is a frequency that decreases across pairs. Values are not rotated.

Since rotating q by angle a and k by angle b changes their dot product only through the difference a − b, attention scores become a function of content and relative offset, without any extra parameters or learned tables. RoPE is applied inside every attention layer rather than added once at the input; LLaMA, Mistral and Qwen all use it. A known limitation is poor extrapolation beyond the trained context length; methods such as position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN rescale the frequencies to extend context, usually with brief fine-tuning.

Extending context length with frequency scaling
Position encoding without extra learned parameters
rope.x: A team extending an open LLM from 8K to 64K context for long-document question answering rescales the RoPE base frequency and fine-tunes briefly on long sequences. They validate on retrieval-style tests that place a key fact at varying depths to confirm the model still uses distant tokens.
rope.c:
import torch

def rope(x, base=10000.0):
    # x: (batch, seq_len, n_heads, head_dim), head_dim even
    B, T, H, D = x.shape
    inv_freq = base ** (-torch.arange(0, D, 2).float() / D)   # (D/2,)
    angles = torch.arange(T).float()[:, None] * inv_freq      # (T, D/2)
    cos, sin = angles.cos()[None, :, None, :], angles.sin()[None, :, None, :]
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]                       # pair dimensions
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2] = x1 * cos - x2 * sin                      # 2D rotation
    out[..., 1::2] = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return out

q = torch.randn(1, 16, 4, 32)
k = torch.randn(1, 16, 4, 32)
q_rot, k_rot = rope(q), rope(k)    # rotate queries and keys only
scores = torch.einsum('bthd,bshd->bhts', q_rot, k_rot) / 32 ** 0.5
print(scores.shape)

alibi.d:
ALiBi encodes position by subtracting a penalty proportional to the distance between query and key directly from the attention scores, instead of adding position vectors to the embeddings. For head h, the score between positions i and j receives a bias of −m_h·(i − j), where m_h is a fixed, head-specific slope taken from a geometric sequence such as 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and so on.

The effect is a built-in recency preference: distant tokens are down-weighted, more strongly in heads with steep slopes and only gently in heads with shallow slopes, so different heads cover different ranges. ALiBi has no learned parameters and was proposed to let models trained on short sequences run on longer ones at inference, which it does better than sinusoidal or learned absolute encodings. The limitation is that the linear penalty biases attention toward nearby context, and in practice extrapolation helps perplexity more than it helps retrieving specific facts from far back in the sequence.

Position encoding with zero parameters
Language models such as BLOOM and MPT
alibi.x: The BLOOM and MPT open model families use ALiBi instead of positional embeddings. A team serving such a model can raise the inference context somewhat beyond the training length without retraining, but they still benchmark long-input tasks because quality degrades gradually as length grows.
alibi.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def alibi_slopes(n_heads):
    # Geometric sequence 2^(-8/n), 2^(-16/n), ...
    return torch.tensor([2 ** (-8 * (h + 1) / n_heads) for h in range(n_heads)])

H, T, d = 4, 6, 16
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, H, T, d) for _ in range(3))
pos = torch.arange(T)
distance = (pos[:, None] - pos[None, :]).clamp(min=0)          # i - j for j <= i
bias = -alibi_slopes(H)[:, None, None] * distance              # (H, T, T)
causal = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), 1)

scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / d ** 0.5 + bias             # add linear penalty
scores = scores.masked_fill(causal, float('-inf'))
out = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ v
print(out.shape)

transformer.d:
A Transformer block is the repeating unit of a Transformer: a multi-head attention sublayer followed by a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization. Attention mixes information across tokens, while the feed-forward network processes each token independently, and the residual connections keep a direct path for information and gradients through deep stacks.

Most modern LLMs use the pre-norm arrangement, where the normalization is applied to the input of each sublayer (x + Attn(Norm(x))), which trains more stably than the original post-norm design. Typical modern variants replace LayerNorm with RMSNorm, use a SwiGLU feed-forward network, and apply RoPE inside attention. Blocks are stacked dozens of times with identical shapes, which makes the architecture easy to scale and parallelize. A common misconception is that attention holds most of the parameters; in standard configurations the feed-forward network holds about two thirds of each block's weights.
transformer.f: h = x + MHA(Norm(x)),  y = h + FFN(Norm(h))

Vision Transformers for image classification
Sequence models for audio, proteins, time series
transformer.x: A speech company builds its recognition encoder from a stack of identical Transformer blocks, which lets the team scale model size by changing only depth and width. Because each block has the same structure, they can apply tensor parallelism and activation checkpointing uniformly across the stack during training.
transformer.c:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model=256, n_heads=8, d_ff=1024, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(d_model, n_heads, dropout=dropout,
                                          batch_first=True)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), nn.GELU(),
                                 nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model), nn.Dropout(dropout))

    def forward(self, x, attn_mask=None):
        h = self.norm1(x)                                   # pre-norm
        x = x + self.attn(h, h, h, attn_mask=attn_mask)[0]  # residual 1
        return x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))                  # residual 2

x = torch.randn(2, 32, 256)
model = nn.Sequential(*[Block() for _ in range(4)])
print(model(x).shape)

encoderonly.d:
Encoder-only models are Transformers that read the whole input with bidirectional self-attention and output a contextual vector for every token, rather than generating text. BERT is the best-known example. Because no causal mask is applied, each token's representation depends on words both before and after it, which gives rich context for understanding tasks.

They are pretrained with objectives that do not require left-to-right generation, mainly masked language modeling, where randomly hidden tokens must be reconstructed. For downstream use, a small head is placed on top: a classifier on the [CLS] or mean-pooled vector for sentence classification, a per-token classifier for named entity recognition, or a span predictor for extractive question answering. Encoder-only models are compact and fast for classification, retrieval embeddings and reranking. Their main limitation is that they are not natural text generators; producing fluent free-form output requires a decoder, which is why chat assistants are built on decoder-only models.
encoderonly.f: hᵢ = Encoder(x₁,…,x_T)ᵢ  (bidirectional: every hᵢ depends on all x_j)

decoderonly.d:
Decoder-only models are Transformers that use causal self-attention and are trained to predict the next token, so they generate text one token at a time conditioned on everything before it. The GPT series, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen and most current chat assistants follow this design. The prompt and the generated output live in a single sequence, with no separate encoder.

Their appeal is simplicity and generality: one objective, next-token prediction on large text corpora, scales well and turns many tasks into text continuation, including translation, summarization, coding and question answering via prompting or instruction tuning. During generation a KV cache stores keys and values of past tokens so each new step costs time proportional to the context length rather than recomputing everything. The main limitations are sequential decoding, which bounds latency per token, and the fact that each token's representation sees only the left context, which can make them less parameter-efficient than bidirectional encoders for pure classification or embedding tasks.

Code completion and generation
Few-shot task solving through prompting

encdec.d:
Encoder-decoder models pair a bidirectional encoder that reads the full input with an autoregressive decoder that generates the output while attending to the encoder through cross-attention. This is the original Transformer layout from machine translation, and T5, BART and Whisper use it as well.

The split suits tasks with a clear input and a distinct output, such as translation, summarization and speech recognition. The encoder processes the source once with full context, and the decoder only has to model the target sequence, which is often shorter. T5 reframed every NLP task as text-to-text, with a task prefix in the input string, and was pretrained with span corruption, where the decoder reconstructs masked spans of the input. A common misconception is that encoder-decoder models are obsolete; they remain competitive and efficient for conditional generation at moderate scale, but decoder-only models are simpler to scale for open-ended chat, which explains their dominance in general-purpose LLMs.
encdec.f: P(y | x) = Πₜ P(yₜ | y<ₜ, Encoder(x))

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(name)

                return_tensors="pt")
tgt = tokenizer(["Budget cuts and hiring were discussed."],
                return_tensors="pt").input_ids

loss.backward()

ffn.d:
The feed-forward network in a Transformer is a two-layer MLP applied to each token independently, expanding the hidden size, applying a nonlinearity and projecting back. In the original design the inner dimension is four times d_model with a ReLU; modern LLMs typically use SwiGLU, a gated variant with three weight matrices where one projection, passed through SiLU, multiplies another elementwise.

Attention moves information between tokens, while the FFN transforms each token's representation in place. Interpretability research suggests FFN layers behave partly like key-value memories that store factual and lexical associations. They account for roughly two thirds of the parameters in a standard block, so they dominate model size and much of the compute. This is also why Mixture-of-Experts models replace the FFN with many expert FFNs and route each token to a few of them. When using SwiGLU, the inner dimension is usually reduced to about 8/3·d_model to keep the parameter count comparable to a 4× ReLU FFN.
ffn.f: FFN(x) = W₂·φ(W₁x + b₁) + b₂;  SwiGLU(x) = W₂·(SiLU(W₁x) ⊙ W₃x)

ffn.c:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, hidden):
        super().__init__()
        self.w1 = nn.Linear(d_model, hidden, bias=False)   # gate projection
        self.w3 = nn.Linear(d_model, hidden, bias=False)   # up projection
        self.w2 = nn.Linear(hidden, d_model, bias=False)   # down projection

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.w2(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w3(x))    # gated, per token

d_model = 512
hidden = -(-int(8 * d_model / 3) // 256) * 256             # ~8/3 d, rounded up
ffn = SwiGLU(d_model, hidden)
x = torch.randn(2, 16, d_model)
print(ffn(x).shape, sum(p.numel() for p in ffn.parameters()))

prenorm.d:
Pre-norm and post-norm differ in where layer normalization sits relative to the residual connection in a Transformer block. Post-norm, used in the original Transformer and BERT, normalizes after the residual addition: x ← Norm(x + F(x)). Pre-norm, used in GPT-2 and nearly all modern LLMs, normalizes only the input to each sublayer: x ← x + F(Norm(x)).

The placement changes gradient flow. In pre-norm the residual stream is an unnormalized identity path from input to output, so gradients reach early layers directly, and deep models train stably without a long learning-rate warmup. Post-norm puts a normalization on that path at every layer, which can cause vanishing or exploding gradients in deep stacks and makes training sensitive to warmup. The trade-off is that pre-norm often reaches slightly worse final quality at equal depth, because the residual stream grows and later layers contribute relatively less. Variants such as DeepNorm and adding a final norm after the last block address these issues.
prenorm.f: Post-norm: x ← Norm(x + F(x));  Pre-norm: x ← x + F(Norm(x))

Reducing dependence on learning-rate warmup
Choosing block layout for new LLM architectures

tokenization.d:
Tokenization converts raw text into a sequence of integer ids from a fixed vocabulary, which is the only form of input a language model actually sees. Modern LLMs use subword tokenizers such as BPE, WordPiece or Unigram, which keep frequent words as single tokens and split rare words into smaller pieces, so any string can be represented without unknown tokens.

The tokenizer is trained before the model and frozen afterward, and it shapes many model properties: sequence length and therefore cost, how numbers and code are split, and how fairly different languages are served. A text in a language underrepresented in the tokenizer's training data may need several times more tokens for the same content, which raises cost and shortens the effective context. A common pitfall is mixing tokenizers and models, or ignoring special tokens and chat templates; a fine-tuned model can behave badly if prompts are not formatted and tokenized exactly as in training.

Estimating API cost and context usage
Building vocabularies for new languages or domains

bpe.d:
Byte-Pair Encoding builds a subword vocabulary by starting from single characters or bytes and repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until a target vocabulary size is reached. The ordered list of merges is the tokenizer: to encode new text, the same merges are applied in the order they were learned.

Frequent words end up as single tokens, while rare words and misspellings decompose into common pieces, which balances vocabulary size against sequence length. Byte-level BPE, used by GPT-2 and many later models, starts from the 256 possible byte values, so any Unicode string can be encoded with no unknown token. Vocabulary size is a key design choice: larger vocabularies shorten sequences but enlarge the embedding and output layers. A known weakness is that merges are driven purely by frequency, so number splitting can be inconsistent, for example a number becoming one token while a neighboring value splits in two, which can hurt arithmetic.
bpe.f: repeat: (a, b) = argmax count(a, b);  replace every 'a b' with new token 'ab'
u: Tokenizers for GPT and LLaMA-family models
Open-vocabulary handling of rare words
Training custom tokenizers for code or domains
bpe.x: A team building a code model trains a byte-level BPE tokenizer on their source corpus so that common indentation runs and keywords become single tokens. This shortens typical files compared with a general-purpose tokenizer, which lowers training cost and lets more code fit in the context window.

from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, trainers, pre_tokenizers, decoders

tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.ByteLevel(add_prefix_space=False)
tokenizer.decoder = decoders.ByteLevel()
trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(vocab_size=300,
                              initial_alphabet=pre_tokenizers.ByteLevel.alphabet())
tokenizer.train_from_iterator(corpus, trainer)   # learn merges by frequency

enc = tokenizer.encode("lowest newest")

print(tokenizer.decode(enc.ids))                 # lossless decoding

mlm.d:
Masked language modeling is a pretraining objective in which some input tokens are hidden and the model learns to predict them from the surrounding context on both sides. In BERT, 15% of token positions are selected; of those, 80% are replaced with a [MASK] token, 10% with a random token and 10% are left unchanged, and the loss is computed only on the selected positions.

Because the model sees both left and right context, it learns strong bidirectional representations that transfer well to classification, tagging and retrieval. The 80/10/10 split exists because [MASK] never appears at fine-tuning time; mixing in random and unchanged tokens forces the model to build useful representations for every token, not only masked ones. A key limitation is efficiency: only about 15% of tokens produce a training signal per pass, which is why ELECTRA's replaced-token detection, which learns from every position, can be more compute-efficient. MLM also does not directly yield a left-to-right text generator.
mlm.f: L_MLM = −Σ_{i∈M} log P(xᵢ | x without positions M)
u: Pretraining BERT and RoBERTa encoders
Domain-adaptive pretraining on in-domain text
Learning protein and genomic sequence representations

                          DataCollatorForLanguageModeling)

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(name)

# Selects 15% of tokens; applies the 80/10/10 mask/random/keep rule
collator = DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tokenizer=tok, mlm=True,
                                           mlm_probability=0.15)
texts = ["The court dismissed the appeal.", "Payment is due within thirty days."]
features = [tok(t, truncation=True, max_length=64) for t in texts]

out.loss.backward()

nexttoken.d:
Next-token prediction trains a language model to output a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the token that follows a given prefix, using cross-entropy against the actual next token. Summed over all positions, this maximizes the likelihood of the training text under the chain rule of probability.

With a causal mask, a single forward pass yields a prediction at every position, so each sequence of length T provides T training signals; the inputs are the tokens and the targets are the same tokens shifted left by one. This simple, self-supervised objective needs no labels and scales to trillions of tokens, and it underlies the pretraining of GPT-style models. Doing it well requires modeling grammar, facts and reasoning patterns present in the data. A common misconception is that the objective only teaches surface statistics; at the same time, it optimizes for plausible continuations rather than truthfulness, so models also need post-training to follow instructions and avoid confident errors.
u: Pretraining decoder-only language models
Continued pretraining on domain corpora
Scoring sequence likelihood and perplexity
nexttoken.x: A financial data provider continues next-token pretraining of an open model on filings and analyst reports before instruction tuning. They track validation perplexity on held-out filings and on general text to make sure domain gains do not come with large losses in general ability.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")

ids = tok("Revenue grew in the third quarter.", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
logits = model(ids).logits                    # (1, T, vocab)

# Shift: position t predicts token t+1
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[:, :-1].reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)),
                       ids[:, 1:].reshape(-1))
print(loss.item(), torch.exp(loss).item())    # loss and perplexity

# The library does the same shift internally when labels=input_ids
print(model(ids, labels=ids).loss.item())

kvcache.d:
A KV cache stores the key and value vectors of all previously processed tokens during autoregressive generation, so each new token only needs to compute its own query, key and value instead of reprocessing the whole sequence. The new query attends over the cached keys and values, and the new key and value are appended to the cache.

Without caching, every step would recompute keys and values for the entire prefix, making total generation cost grow roughly quadratically in the projections and cubically in attention; with it, each decoding step does work proportional to the current length. The cost moves to memory: the cache size is 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × sequence length × batch size × bytes per value, which for long contexts and large batches can exceed the model weights. This memory, not compute, often limits serving throughput, which motivates grouped-query attention, cache quantization, and paged memory management as in vLLM's PagedAttention.
kvcache.f: Memory = 2 · n_layers · n_kv_heads · d_head · seq_len · batch · bytes
u: Fast autoregressive decoding in LLM serving
Prefix caching for shared system prompts
Capacity planning for long-context inference
kvcache.x: An LLM serving team uses vLLM, whose PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks to reduce fragmentation and allow sharing of common prompt prefixes. They size GPU memory by computing cache bytes per token for the model and set the maximum batch and context so the cache fits.
kvcache.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
d = 32
W_q, W_k, W_v = (torch.randn(d, d) / d ** 0.5 for _ in range(3))
k_cache, v_cache = [], []

def decode_step(x_t):
    # x_t: (1, d) hidden state of the newest token only
    q = x_t @ W_q
    k_cache.append(x_t @ W_k)                 # append new key
    v_cache.append(x_t @ W_v)                 # append new value
    K, V = torch.cat(k_cache), torch.cat(v_cache)   # (t, d) from cache
    w = F.softmax(q @ K.T / d ** 0.5, dim=-1)
    return w @ V

for t in range(5):
    out = decode_step(torch.randn(1, d))
print(out.shape, len(k_cache))

# Cache size for a 32-layer model, 8 KV heads, d_head 128, 8K tokens, fp16
print(2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 8192 * 2 / 2**30, "GiB per sequence")

flashattn.d:
FlashAttention is an exact attention algorithm that computes the same result as standard attention but never writes the full T×T score matrix to GPU high-bandwidth memory. It splits queries, keys and values into tiles that fit in fast on-chip SRAM, computes partial softmax results tile by tile, and combines them using an online softmax that tracks a running maximum and normalizer for each row.

Standard attention is limited by memory traffic rather than arithmetic: reading and writing the large score and probability matrices dominates runtime. By fusing the matmul, masking, softmax and the multiplication by V into one kernel, FlashAttention reduces memory use from quadratic to linear in sequence length and gives large wall-clock speedups, especially for long contexts. In the backward pass it recomputes attention tiles instead of storing them. A common misconception is that it is an approximation; it is mathematically exact and lowers memory, but it does not change the quadratic number of operations.
flashattn.f: mₙ = max(mₙ₋₁, max sₙ),  ℓₙ = e^(mₙ₋₁−mₙ)·ℓₙ₋₁ + Σ e^(sₙ−mₙ)
u: Speeding up LLM training on long sequences
Reducing attention memory during inference prefill
Enabling longer context on fixed GPU memory
flashattn.x: A team pretraining a 7B model switches its attention implementation to FlashAttention through PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention. The lower activation memory lets them double sequence length without changing the batch size, and they confirm numerically that outputs match the reference implementation within bf16 tolerance.
flashattn.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def tiled_attention(q, k, v, tile=64):
    # Online softmax over key tiles: exact result, no full T x T matrix stored
    T, d = q.shape
    m = torch.full((T, 1), float('-inf'))     # running row max
    l = torch.zeros(T, 1)                     # running normalizer
    acc = torch.zeros(T, d)                   # running weighted sum of V
    for s in range(0, k.shape[0], tile):
        scores = q @ k[s:s+tile].T / d ** 0.5
        m_new = torch.maximum(m, scores.max(dim=1, keepdim=True).values)
        p = torch.exp(scores - m_new)
        scale = torch.exp(m - m_new)          # rescale old statistics
        l = scale * l + p.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
        acc = scale * acc + p @ v[s:s+tile]
        m = m_new
    return acc / l

q, k, v = (torch.randn(256, 32) for _ in range(3))
ref = F.softmax(q @ k.T / 32 ** 0.5, dim=-1) @ v
print(torch.allclose(tiled_attention(q, k, v), ref, atol=1e-5))

mqa.d:
Multi-query attention keeps many query heads but shares a single key head and a single value head across all of them. Each query head still computes its own attention pattern, but all heads read from the same keys and values.

The motivation is inference speed. During autoregressive decoding, each step must load the entire KV cache from memory, and that memory traffic, not arithmetic, usually limits throughput. With h query heads, MQA shrinks the KV cache and its bandwidth cost by a factor of h compared with standard multi-head attention, which allows larger batches and longer contexts on the same hardware. It was used in models such as PaLM and Falcon. The trade-off is quality and training stability: sharing one key-value head reduces model capacity, and converting an existing multi-head model to MQA typically requires additional training. Grouped-query attention was introduced as a middle ground that recovers most of the quality while keeping most of the savings.
mqa.f: headᵢ = Attention(QWᵢ_Q, K W_K, V W_V)  (one shared W_K, W_V for all i)
u: Reducing KV-cache memory in LLM serving
Higher decoding throughput at large batch sizes
Long-context inference on limited GPU memory
mqa.x: A team serving a chat model on memory-constrained GPUs chooses an MQA architecture so the KV cache for each conversation is a fraction of the multi-head size. The smaller cache lets each GPU hold many more concurrent sessions, at the cost of a small quality gap they track on internal benchmarks.
mqa.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
B, T, d_model, n_heads = 2, 12, 64, 8
d_head = d_model // n_heads
x = torch.randn(B, T, d_model)

W_q = torch.nn.Linear(d_model, n_heads * d_head, bias=False)  # many query heads
W_k = torch.nn.Linear(d_model, d_head, bias=False)            # ONE key head
W_v = torch.nn.Linear(d_model, d_head, bias=False)            # ONE value head

q = W_q(x).view(B, T, n_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 2)        # (B, h, T, d)
k = W_k(x).unsqueeze(1)                                       # (B, 1, T, d)
v = W_v(x).unsqueeze(1)
# Broadcasting shares the single K/V head across all query heads
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k.expand_as(q), v.expand_as(q),
                                     is_causal=True)
print(out.shape)
print("KV cache per token:", 2 * d_head, "vs MHA:", 2 * n_heads * d_head)

gqa.d:
Grouped-query attention divides the query heads into groups and gives each group its own shared key and value head, sitting between multi-head attention (one KV head per query head) and multi-query attention (one KV head for all). With 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, for example, every 4 query heads share one key-value pair.

The KV cache shrinks by the ratio of query heads to KV heads, which cuts the memory bandwidth needed per decoding step and allows larger batches or longer contexts. Experiments in the original paper showed that GQA reaches quality close to full multi-head attention with speed close to MQA, and existing multi-head checkpoints can be converted by mean-pooling key and value heads within each group and then briefly continuing training. GQA is now standard in LLaMA 2 70B and later LLaMA models, Mistral and many other LLMs. It reduces cache size but not the attention compute for the prefill of long prompts.
gqa.f: KV-cache reduction = n_q_heads / n_kv_heads;  group(i) = ⌊i · n_kv / n_q⌋
u: Standard attention layout in modern open LLMs
Shrinking KV cache with minimal quality loss
Uptraining multi-head checkpoints for faster inference
gqa.x: Meta's LLaMA 2 70B and the LLaMA 3 models use grouped-query attention with 8 key-value heads. A company self-hosting such a model benefits directly, because the smaller per-token cache lets each GPU serve more concurrent requests at long context lengths.
gqa.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
B, T, d_head = 2, 16, 32
n_q, n_kv = 8, 2                          # 4 query heads share each KV head
group = n_q // n_kv

q = torch.randn(B, n_q, T, d_head)
k = torch.randn(B, n_kv, T, d_head)       # only n_kv heads are cached
v = torch.randn(B, n_kv, T, d_head)

# Repeat each KV head for the query heads in its group
k_rep = k.repeat_interleave(group, dim=1)  # (B, n_q, T, d_head)
v_rep = v.repeat_interleave(group, dim=1)
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k_rep, v_rep, is_causal=True)
print(out.shape)
print("cache reduction vs MHA:", n_q // n_kv, "x")

swa.d:
Sliding window attention restricts each token to attend only to the previous w tokens instead of the entire sequence, turning attention into a local band. Compute and KV-cache memory therefore grow linearly with sequence length for a fixed window, rather than quadratically for compute and linearly with the full context for the cache.

Information can still travel beyond the window through depth. After one layer a token sees w positions back; after L stacked layers its receptive field reaches about L × w positions, similar to how stacked convolutions grow their receptive field. Mistral 7B uses a 4,096-token window with a rolling buffer cache that overwrites the oldest entries, and models such as Gemma 2 alternate local sliding-window layers with global attention layers. The limitation is that indirect, multi-hop propagation is lossy: precise retrieval of a fact far outside the window is much weaker than with full attention, which is why many designs keep some global layers.
swa.f: Aᵢⱼ allowed iff i − w < j ≤ i;  receptive field ≈ L · w
u: Bounding KV-cache size for long inputs
Efficient long-document encoding with local context
Hybrid local/global attention in modern LLMs
swa.x: A team deploying a model for streaming meeting transcription uses sliding window layers so the KV cache stays fixed in size however long the meeting runs. They interleave a few global attention layers so the model can still refer back to agenda items mentioned at the start.
swa.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def sliding_window_mask(T, window):
    i = torch.arange(T)[:, None]
    j = torch.arange(T)[None, :]
    allowed = (j <= i) & (j > i - window)      # causal band of width w
    return allowed

T, window, d = 10, 3, 16
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 2, T, d) for _ in range(3))
mask = sliding_window_mask(T, window)
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=mask)  # True = keep
print(mask.int())
print(out.shape)
# With L layers, information can travel about L * window positions
print("receptive field after 4 layers:", 4 * window)

sparseattn.d:
Sparse attention computes attention scores for only a selected subset of query-key pairs instead of all T² pairs, reducing cost for long sequences. The subset is defined by a pattern: local windows, strided positions, a few global tokens that attend to and are attended by everything, random links, or content-based selection such as hashing or learned top-k routing.

Fixed patterns from models such as the Sparse Transformer, Longformer and BigBird bring the cost close to linear in sequence length while keeping paths between any two tokens through a small number of hops or global tokens. They work well for long documents, genomic sequences and high-resolution inputs. The difficulty is practical efficiency: irregular sparsity maps poorly to GPU hardware, so theoretical savings only materialize with block-sparse kernels. A second limitation is that a fixed pattern can miss an important long-range dependency that full attention would capture, so many recent long-context LLMs prefer dense attention with FlashAttention plus selective sparse layers.
sparseattn.f: Attention restricted to S: Aᵢ = softmax({qᵢ·kⱼ/√d : j ∈ Sᵢ}),  |Sᵢ| ≪ T
u: Long document classification and question answering
Genomic and other very long sequences
High-resolution image or video Transformers
sparseattn.x: A biotech team models DNA sequences tens of thousands of bases long with a BigBird-style encoder that combines local windows, global tokens and random links. Full attention at that length would not fit in GPU memory, and the block-sparse pattern keeps training throughput acceptable.
sparseattn.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def longformer_style_mask(T, window, global_idx):
    i = torch.arange(T)[:, None]
    j = torch.arange(T)[None, :]
    mask = (i - j).abs() <= window          # local band (bidirectional)
    mask[global_idx, :] = True              # global tokens see everything
    mask[:, global_idx] = True              # and everything sees them
    return mask

T, d = 32, 16
mask = longformer_style_mask(T, window=2, global_idx=[0])
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 1, T, d) for _ in range(3))
out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=mask)
print(out.shape)
print("fraction of pairs computed:", mask.float().mean().item())

linattn.d:
Linear attention replaces the softmax similarity with a kernel feature map φ so that attention can be computed in time linear in sequence length. Writing sim(q, k) = φ(q)·φ(k), the output for query i becomes φ(qᵢ)ᵀ(Σⱼ φ(kⱼ)vⱼᵀ) divided by φ(qᵢ)ᵀΣⱼ φ(kⱼ); by associativity, the sums over keys can be computed once and reused for every query.

In the causal case these sums become a running state that is updated with each new token, so the model behaves like a recurrent network with a fixed-size d×d memory, giving constant memory per generated token and no growing KV cache. This idea underlies Performer, RetNet, and the connection between attention and state-space models such as Mamba. The main limitation is quality: a fixed-size state cannot store arbitrary amounts of context, so pure linear attention typically lags softmax attention on precise recall tasks. Modern variants add decay or gating, and many hybrids keep some full attention layers.
linattn.f: oᵢ = φ(qᵢ)ᵀ Sᵢ / φ(qᵢ)ᵀ zᵢ,  Sᵢ = Sᵢ₋₁ + φ(kᵢ)vᵢᵀ,  zᵢ = zᵢ₋₁ + φ(kᵢ)
u: Autoregressive generation with constant memory per token
Very long sequence modeling at linear cost
Hybrid recurrent-attention language model layers
linattn.x: An on-device assistant team experiments with a hybrid model whose layers are mostly gated linear attention plus a few full attention layers. The recurrent state keeps memory flat during long conversations on a phone, while the full attention layers preserve accurate recall of recent details.
linattn.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def phi(x):
    return F.elu(x) + 1                     # positive feature map

def causal_linear_attention(q, k, v):
    T, d = q.shape
    S = torch.zeros(d, v.shape[1])          # running sum of phi(k) v^T
    z = torch.zeros(d)                      # running sum of phi(k)
    out = []
    for t in range(T):                      # recurrent form: O(T) total
        S = S + torch.outer(phi(k[t]), v[t])
        z = z + phi(k[t])
        out.append(phi(q[t]) @ S / (phi(q[t]) @ z + 1e-6))
    return torch.stack(out)

q, k, v = (torch.randn(50, 16) for _ in range(3))
o = causal_linear_attention(q, k, v)
print(o.shape)   # state size is d x d_v, independent of sequence length

scaling.d:
Scaling laws are empirical relationships showing that a language model's test loss decreases as a smooth power law in the number of parameters, the amount of training data and the training compute, when the other factors are not the bottleneck. Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI observed these trends across several orders of magnitude, and later work refined them.

Their practical value is prediction and planning. By training a series of small models and fitting the curve, a team can estimate the loss of a much larger run before spending the compute, choose model size and token count for a fixed budget, and compare architectures or data mixtures by how their curves shift. The laws describe pretraining loss, not every downstream ability: some benchmark scores change abruptly or plateau even when loss improves smoothly. Another pitfall is extrapolating too far or across changes in data quality, tokenizer or architecture; fitted exponents are specific to the setup they were measured in.
u: Forecasting loss of large training runs
Choosing model size for a compute budget
Comparing architectures and data mixtures fairly
scaling.x: Before committing to a large pretraining run, an LLM team trains a ladder of models from tens of millions to a few billion parameters on the same data. They fit a power law to the final losses and use it to choose the size and token count of the flagship run, then check the prediction against early checkpoints.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

# Final losses from a ladder of small runs (toy numbers)
N = np.array([2e7, 6e7, 2e8, 6e8, 2e9])          # parameters
L = np.array([4.10, 3.72, 3.38, 3.12, 2.90])     # validation loss

def power_law(n, E, A, alpha):
    return E + A / n ** alpha                    # irreducible loss + power law

params, _ = curve_fit(power_law, N, L, p0=[1.5, 400.0, 0.3], maxfev=20000)
E, A, alpha = params
print(f"E={E:.2f}, A={A:.1f}, alpha={alpha:.3f}")

for n in [7e9, 7e10]:                            # extrapolate with caution
    print(f"{n:.0e} params -> predicted loss {power_law(n, *params):.2f}")

chinchilla.d:
Chinchilla-optimal training is the rule that, for a fixed training compute budget, model parameters and training tokens should be scaled in roughly equal proportion, which works out to about 20 tokens per parameter. DeepMind's Chinchilla paper showed that many earlier large models were undertrained: a 70B-parameter model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens outperformed the 280B Gopher model trained with the same compute.

The analysis uses training compute C ≈ 6ND, where N is parameters and D is tokens, and finds that the loss-minimizing N and D each grow roughly as the square root of C. A frequent misconception is that 20 tokens per parameter is the best target for every project. It minimizes training compute for a given loss, but it ignores inference cost. Models that will serve heavy traffic, such as the LLaMA series, are deliberately trained far beyond this ratio, because a smaller model trained on more data is cheaper to run for its whole lifetime.
chinchilla.f: C ≈ 6·N·D,  N_opt ∝ C^0.5,  D_opt ∝ C^0.5,  D_opt ≈ 20·N_opt
u: Allocating compute between model size and data
Planning token budgets for pretraining runs
Judging whether a model is undertrained
chinchilla.x: A startup with a fixed GPU budget uses the Chinchilla ratio as a starting point, then deliberately trains a smaller model on several times more tokens. Because the model will serve millions of requests, they accept higher training cost per unit of quality in exchange for lower inference cost.
chinchilla.c:
def chinchilla_optimal(compute_flops, tokens_per_param=20.0):
    # C = 6 N D and D = k N  ->  N = sqrt(C / (6 k))
    n = (compute_flops / (6 * tokens_per_param)) ** 0.5
    return n, tokens_per_param * n

for C in [1e21, 1e23, 5.76e23]:            # last one ~ Chinchilla's budget
    n, d = chinchilla_optimal(C)
    print(f"C={C:.2e}  params={n/1e9:6.1f}B  tokens={d/1e9:8.0f}B")

# Inference-heavy choice: smaller model, more tokens, same compute
C = 1e23
n_small = 3e9
d_small = C / (6 * n_small)
print(f"3B model at same compute trains on {d_small/1e9:.0f}B tokens "
      f"({d_small / n_small:.0f} tokens/param)")

icl.d:
In-context learning is the ability of a large language model to perform a new task from instructions or a few examples placed in the prompt, without any update to its weights. Given several input-output demonstrations followed by a new input, the model continues the pattern, and the same frozen model can switch tasks just by changing the prompt.

This ability emerged at scale with GPT-3. Research suggests the model infers the task format and label space from the demonstrations, and mechanisms such as induction heads, which copy patterns seen earlier in the context, contribute to it. Performance depends heavily on the choice, order and format of examples, and selecting demonstrations similar to the query through retrieval often helps. A notable finding is that models sometimes rely more on format and label distribution than on whether the example labels are correct. In-context learning is limited by context length and costs tokens on every call, unlike fine-tuning.
icl.f: ŷ = argmax_y P_θ(y | x₁, y₁, …, x_k, y_k, x)  (θ fixed)
u: Few-shot classification without fine-tuning
Rapid prototyping of new LLM-powered features
Format-following via example demonstrations
icl.x: A marketplace team builds a product categorization prototype by placing ten labeled examples, retrieved by embedding similarity to each new listing, into the prompt of a hosted LLM. This avoids training a model during exploration, and they move to fine-tuning only once volume makes the long prompts too costly.

from transformers import pipeline

generator = pipeline("text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")

demos = [("The battery died after two days.", "negative"),
         ("Setup took one minute, works great.", "positive"),
         ("Arrived on time, nothing special.", "neutral")]
query = "Screen is bright but the speaker crackles."

# Few-shot prompt: the task is defined entirely by the examples
prompt = "Classify the sentiment of each review.\n\n"
for text, label in demos:
    prompt += f"Review: {text}\nSentiment: {label}\n\n"
prompt += f"Review: {query}\nSentiment:"

out = generator(prompt, max_new_tokens=3, do_sample=False,
                return_full_text=False)
print(out[0]["generated_text"].strip())   # no weights were updated

pretrain.d:
Pretraining is the first and most expensive stage of building a foundation model, in which the model learns general representations from a very large unlabeled corpus using a self-supervised objective. For LLMs this is next-token prediction over trillions of tokens of web text, books, code and other sources; for encoders such as BERT it is masked language modeling.

The quality of the result depends as much on data as on architecture. Pipelines deduplicate documents, filter low-quality and toxic text with heuristics and classifiers, remove benchmark contamination, and tune the mixture of domains and languages. Training runs for weeks on thousands of accelerators with data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, careful learning-rate schedules and monitoring for loss spikes. The resulting base model can complete text and has broad knowledge, but it does not reliably follow instructions; post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization is what turns it into a usable assistant. Knowledge learned in pretraining also has a fixed cutoff date.
pretrain.f: θ* = argmin_θ E_{x∼D} [−Σₜ log P_θ(xₜ | x<ₜ)]
u: Building base LLMs from web-scale text
Continued pretraining on domain or language data
Self-supervised encoders for vision and speech

from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import (AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, Trainer,
                          TrainingArguments, DataCollatorForLanguageModeling)

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")

raw = load_dataset("wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1", split="train")
data = raw.map(lambda b: tok(b["text"], truncation=True, max_length=512),
               batched=True, remove_columns=["text"])
data = data.filter(lambda ex: len(ex["input_ids"]) > 16)   # drop tiny lines

collator = DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tok, mlm=False)  # next-token labels
args = TrainingArguments("pretrain-out", per_device_train_batch_size=8,
                         learning_rate=3e-4, lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
                         warmup_ratio=0.02, bf16=True, max_steps=1000)
Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=data,
        data_collator=collator).train()

sft.d:
Supervised fine-tuning trains a pretrained language model on curated prompt-response pairs so that it learns to follow instructions and produce responses in a desired style. The objective is still next-token cross-entropy, but the loss is usually computed only on the response tokens, with the prompt tokens masked out, so the model learns to answer rather than to imitate user messages.

SFT is typically the first post-training step after pretraining. A few thousand to a few hundred thousand high-quality examples, formatted with the model's chat template, are often enough to change behavior substantially, because the model already has the underlying knowledge. Data quality and diversity matter more than volume. SFT is also used to specialize models for domains or output formats such as JSON. Its limitations are that it only imitates demonstrations, so it cannot easily teach the model to prefer better answers over merely plausible ones, and that aggressive fine-tuning on narrow data can cause forgetting of general abilities.
sft.f: L_SFT = −Σ_{t ∈ response} log P_θ(yₜ | prompt, y<ₜ)
u: Turning base models into instruction followers
Teaching structured output formats such as JSON
Domain specialization for support or legal tasks
sft.x: An insurance company fine-tunes an open LLM on several thousand reviewed question-answer pairs about its policies, formatted with the model's chat template. They mask the prompt tokens from the loss and evaluate on a held-out set plus general benchmarks to catch any loss of broader ability.

rlhf.d:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback aligns a language model with human preferences by training it to maximize a learned reward that predicts which responses people prefer. The classic pipeline, used for InstructGPT and early ChatGPT, has three stages: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, training a reward model on human comparisons between pairs of responses, and optimizing the policy against that reward with PPO.

Comparisons are easier for people to provide reliably than ideal answers, and the reward model generalizes those judgments to new prompts. During RL a KL penalty keeps the policy close to the SFT reference model, which preserves fluency and limits exploitation of reward-model errors. RLHF improves helpfulness, harmlessness and instruction following beyond what SFT achieves. Its weaknesses are cost and fragility: it needs several models in memory, many hyperparameters, and is prone to reward hacking, where the policy learns quirks such as excessive length or flattery that the reward model scores highly but people do not actually prefer.
rlhf.f: max_π E_{x, y∼π} [r_φ(x, y)] − β·KL(π(·|x) ‖ π_ref(·|x))
u: Aligning chat assistants with human preferences
Reducing harmful or unhelpful responses
Improving summarization quality beyond imitation
rlhf.x: OpenAI described using RLHF to train InstructGPT, where labelers ranked model outputs and a reward model trained on those rankings guided PPO. Teams applying the same recipe monitor response length and reward-model scores together, because a rising reward with steadily longer answers is a common sign of reward hacking.
rlhf.c:
import torch

def rlhf_reward(rm_score, logp_policy, logp_ref, beta=0.05):
    # Sequence reward = reward model score - beta * KL estimate
    kl = (logp_policy - logp_ref).sum(dim=-1)   # sum over generated tokens
    return rm_score - beta * kl

# Toy batch: 4 responses, 12 generated tokens each
rm_score = torch.tensor([1.2, 0.3, 2.0, -0.5])        # from the reward model
logp_policy = torch.randn(4, 12) * 0.1 - 2.0          # current policy log-probs
logp_ref = torch.randn(4, 12) * 0.1 - 2.0             # frozen SFT model log-probs

r = rlhf_reward(rm_score, logp_policy, logp_ref)
print(r)   # this reward is what PPO maximizes

# In practice, TRL's PPOTrainer runs the full loop:
# policy, reference model, reward model and value model

rewardmodel.d:
A reward model is a network that takes a prompt and a response and outputs a scalar score estimating how much humans, or another judge, would prefer that response. It is usually a pretrained language model with a single linear output head, trained on pairwise comparisons where one response was chosen over another.

The standard training loss is the Bradley-Terry objective: maximize the log-sigmoid of the score difference between the chosen and the rejected response. Only differences matter, so the absolute scale of rewards is arbitrary. Reward models drive RLHF, rank candidate responses in best-of-n sampling, and filter synthetic data. Their main weakness is that they are imperfect proxies trained on limited data. When a policy is optimized hard against a reward model, it finds inputs where the model is wrong, such as verbose or sycophantic answers, which is called reward hacking or overoptimization. Ensembles, KL constraints and fresh comparison data reduce this risk.
u: Scoring responses for RLHF policy optimization
Best-of-n reranking of sampled answers
Filtering synthetic training data by quality
rewardmodel.x: A team building a coding assistant trains a reward model on developer preferences between pairs of suggested code edits. Besides using it for RL, they use it at inference to rerank several sampled candidates, and they audit cases where it prefers longer code to check for a length bias.
rewardmodel.c:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification

name = "distilroberta-base"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
rm = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=1)

prompt = "How do I reverse a list in Python?"
chosen = prompt + " Use my_list[::-1] or my_list.reverse() for in-place."
rejected = prompt + " You cannot reverse lists in Python."

batch = tok([chosen, rejected], return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
scores = rm(**batch).logits.squeeze(-1)          # one scalar per response
# Bradley-Terry loss: chosen should score higher than rejected
loss = -F.logsigmoid(scores[0] - scores[1])
loss.backward()
print(scores.tolist(), loss.item())

ppo.d:
Proximal Policy Optimization is a policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm that improves a policy while preventing each update from moving it too far from the policy that collected the data. It does this with a clipped objective: the probability ratio between the new and old policy for each action is multiplied by the advantage, but the ratio is clipped to a range such as 0.8 to 1.2, so there is no incentive to push it further.

PPO is popular because it is stable, reuses each batch of experience for several epochs, and is simpler than trust-region methods. A learned value function with generalized advantage estimation supplies advantages. In LLM training, each generated token is an action, the reward arrives at the end of the response, and a per-token KL penalty to a reference model is added. The main drawback for LLMs is cost: policy, value, reward and reference models must all fit in memory, and results depend heavily on hyperparameters.
u: RLHF policy optimization for language models
Robotics and continuous control tasks
Game-playing agents with simulated environments
ppo.x: OpenAI used PPO to train game-playing agents in OpenAI Five and later for the RL stage of InstructGPT. Teams running PPO on LLMs typically watch the clip fraction and the KL to the reference model each step, and stop or lower the learning rate when either grows too quickly.
ppo.c:
import torch

def ppo_loss(logp_new, logp_old, advantages, eps=0.2):
    ratio = torch.exp(logp_new - logp_old)              # pi_new / pi_old
    unclipped = ratio * advantages
    clipped = torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * advantages
    return -torch.min(unclipped, clipped).mean()        # maximize the minimum

torch.manual_seed(0)
logp_old = torch.randn(64) - 1.0                        # from rollout policy
logp_new = (logp_old + 0.1 * torch.randn(64)).requires_grad_()
advantages = torch.randn(64)                            # e.g. from GAE
advantages = (advantages - advantages.mean()) / (advantages.std() + 1e-8)

loss = ppo_loss(logp_new, logp_old, advantages)
loss.backward()
clip_frac = ((torch.exp(logp_new - logp_old) - 1).abs() > 0.2).float().mean()
print(loss.item(), clip_frac.item())

dpo.d:
Direct Preference Optimization trains a language model on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss, without training a separate reward model or running reinforcement learning. It relies on the fact that the optimal policy for the KL-regularized RLHF objective has a closed form, so the reward can be written through the log-probability ratio between the policy and a frozen reference model.

Substituting that implicit reward into the Bradley-Terry preference model yields a loss that increases the policy's relative likelihood of the chosen response over the rejected one, compared with the reference model. The temperature β controls how far the policy may move from the reference. DPO is stable, needs two models in memory and is a standard alignment step for open models. Its limitations are that it learns from a fixed offline dataset, so it cannot explore or correct mistakes outside that data, and it can reduce the absolute likelihood of both chosen and rejected responses, sometimes degrading outputs.
u: Preference alignment of open chat models
Tuning style or tone from pairwise feedback
Reducing unwanted behaviors without RL infrastructure
dpo.x: A team aligning an open model for internal use collects pairwise preferences from domain experts and runs DPO with TRL on top of their SFT checkpoint. They choose DPO over PPO because it fits on fewer GPUs and has fewer hyperparameters, and they compare win rates against the SFT model on held-out prompts.

from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig

name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)

# Each row: prompt, chosen, rejected
dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized", split="train[:2000]")

config = DPOConfig(
    output_dir="dpo-out",
    beta=0.1,                        # strength of the pull toward the reference
    learning_rate=5e-7,
    per_device_train_batch_size=2,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=8,
    bf16=True,
)
trainer = DPOTrainer(model=model, args=config, train_dataset=dataset,
                     processing_class=tokenizer)   # reference = frozen copy
trainer.train()

grpo.d:
Group Relative Policy Optimization is a variant of PPO for language models that removes the learned value function and instead computes each response's advantage relative to a group of responses sampled for the same prompt. For every prompt, the policy generates G completions, each is scored, and the advantage of a completion is its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation.

Using the group as a baseline saves the memory and compute of a separate critic, which is often as large as the policy, and suits rewards given at the end of a response, such as math answer checks. The policy update keeps PPO's clipped ratio and adds a KL penalty to a reference model. GRPO was introduced in DeepSeekMath and used to train DeepSeek-R1's reasoning. A practical limitation is that prompts where all sampled answers receive the same reward give zero advantage and no learning signal, so prompt difficulty must suit the model.
u: Reasoning training with verifiable math rewards
Code generation optimized against unit tests
Critic-free RL fine-tuning on limited GPUs
grpo.x: DeepSeek used GRPO to train its R1 reasoning models with rule-based rewards for answer correctness and format. Teams reproducing this filter their prompt sets so that the model solves some but not all samples per prompt, since groups with uniform rewards contribute nothing to the gradient.
grpo.c:
from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import GRPOTrainer, GRPOConfig

dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/tldr", split="train[:2000]")   # column: prompt

def reward_len(completions, **kwargs):
    # Toy verifiable reward: prefer completions close to 200 characters
    return [-abs(200 - len(c)) / 100 for c in completions]

config = GRPOConfig(
    output_dir="grpo-out",
    num_generations=8,              # group size G per prompt
    max_completion_length=128,
    learning_rate=1e-6,
    beta=0.04,                      # KL penalty to the reference model
    per_device_train_batch_size=8,
    bf16=True,
)
trainer = GRPOTrainer(model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
                      reward_funcs=reward_len, args=config,
                      train_dataset=dataset)
trainer.train()

rlvr.d:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains a language model using rewards computed by a program that checks the output, instead of a learned reward model. Typical verifiers compare a final math answer with the ground truth, run generated code against unit tests, or check that an output satisfies a format or constraint.

Because the reward is objective, it cannot be flattered by style or length in the way a learned reward model can, which allows long RL runs with less reward hacking. Combined with algorithms such as PPO or GRPO, RLVR is the main recipe behind recent reasoning models: the model learns to produce long chains of thought that end in correct answers, and behaviors such as self-checking and backtracking can emerge. The limitation is coverage: it only works for tasks with reliable automatic checks. Lenient verifiers can still be gamed, and sparse binary rewards give no signal on problems the model never solves.
rlvr.f: r(x, y) = 𝟙[verify(x, y) = true];  max_π E[r] − β·KL(π ‖ π_ref)
u: Training math reasoning with checkable answers
Code generation rewarded by passing tests
Instruction following with programmatic constraint checks
rlvr.x: DeepSeek-R1 was trained largely with rule-based rewards that check final answers and output format. A team applying RLVR to SQL generation executes each generated query against a test database and rewards exact result matches, sandboxing execution so generated queries cannot modify data.
rlvr.c:
import re

def extract_answer(text):
    m = re.search(r"\\boxed\{([^}]*)\}", text)    # answer in \boxed{...}
    return m.group(1).strip() if m else None

def math_reward(completions, answer, **kwargs):
    # 1.0 if the final answer matches the ground truth, else 0.0
    return [1.0 if extract_answer(c) == str(a) else 0.0
            for c, a in zip(completions, answer)]

def format_reward(completions, **kwargs):
    return [0.2 if "<think>" in c and "</think>" in c else 0.0
            for c in completions]

samples = ["<think>2+3=5</think> \\boxed{5}", "The answer is 6"]
print(math_reward(samples, answer=[5, 5]))     # [1.0, 0.0]
print(format_reward(samples))                  # [0.2, 0.0]
# Pass both functions as reward_funcs to trl.GRPOTrainer

cai.d:
Constitutional AI is a method from Anthropic for training a harmless and helpful assistant using a written set of principles, the constitution, and AI-generated feedback instead of human labels for harmfulness. RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, is the general idea of replacing human preference labels with judgments from a language model.

The method has two phases. In the supervised phase, the model responds to difficult prompts, then critiques and revises its own responses according to randomly selected principles, and is fine-tuned on the revised answers. In the RL phase, an AI model compares response pairs against the principles, and these AI preferences train a reward model that the policy is optimized against. This scales feedback cheaply and makes the target behavior explicit and auditable through the written principles. The limitation is that quality is bounded by the judging model's ability and biases, so errors or blind spots in the AI feedback can be reinforced rather than corrected.
cai.f: Preference label: y_w = argmax_{y∈{y₁,y₂}} P_judge(y better | x, principles)
u: Harmlessness training without large human labeling
Scaling preference data with LLM judges
Making target behavior explicit through principles
cai.x: Anthropic introduced Constitutional AI to train Claude models to avoid harmful outputs while remaining helpful and willing to explain refusals. Other teams adopt RLAIF by using a strong model as judge to label preference pairs, then spot-check a sample with human reviewers to measure agreement.

from transformers import pipeline

judge = pipeline("text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct")

principle = "Choose the response that is more helpful while avoiding harm."
prompt = "How can I get into my neighbor's wifi?"
a = "Ask your neighbor for the password or use your own provider."
b = "Try common passwords until one works."

query = (f"Principle: {principle}\nUser: {prompt}\n"
         f"Response A: {a}\nResponse B: {b}\n"
         "Which response better follows the principle? Answer A or B.")
msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": query}]
out = judge(msgs, max_new_tokens=3, do_sample=False)
verdict = out[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"].strip()

# AI-labeled pair becomes training data for a reward model or DPO
pair = {"prompt": prompt, "chosen": a if verdict.startswith("A") else b,
        "rejected": b if verdict.startswith("A") else a}
print(pair["chosen"])

lora.d:
LoRA fine-tunes a large model by freezing its original weights and learning a low-rank update for selected weight matrices. For a frozen matrix W of shape d×k, it adds a product BA, where B is d×r and A is r×k with a small rank r such as 8 or 16; only A and B are trained, and the update is scaled by α/r.

Fine-tuning updates tend to have low intrinsic rank. LoRA cuts trainable parameters by orders of magnitude, reduces optimizer memory accordingly, and yields small adapter files that can be swapped on one shared base model. B is initialized to zero so training starts exactly from the base model, and after training BA can be merged into W with no added latency. Targeting all linear layers usually beats targeting only the attention projections. A limitation is that low rank can underfit tasks that require large changes, such as learning new languages or substantial new knowledge.
lora.f: W' = W + (α/r)·B·A,  B ∈ ℝ^(d×r), A ∈ ℝ^(r×k), r ≪ min(d, k)
u: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large LLMs
Serving many task adapters on one base model
Customizing diffusion models for styles or subjects
lora.x: A SaaS company serves one base LLM and loads a separate LoRA adapter for each enterprise customer's tone and terminology. Serving engines such as vLLM can batch requests that use different adapters together, so adding a customer costs only a small adapter file rather than a full model copy.

from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B")

config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,                              # rank of the update
    lora_alpha=32,                     # scale = alpha / r
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
                    "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",

model.print_trainable_parameters()     # well under 1% of all parameters

# ... train with Trainer or SFTTrainer ...
merged = model.merge_and_unload()      # fold BA into W for zero-overhead serving

qlora.d:
QLoRA fine-tunes a large language model by keeping the frozen base weights in 4-bit precision and training LoRA adapters in 16-bit on top of them. Gradients flow through the quantized weights, dequantized on the fly for each matrix multiplication, into the small adapters, which are the only trainable parameters.

Three techniques make this work. NF4 is a 4-bit data type whose levels are placed at quantiles of a normal distribution, matching how pretrained weights are distributed. Double quantization also quantizes the per-block scaling constants to save further memory. Paged optimizers move optimizer state to CPU memory during memory spikes. Together they made it possible to fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU with quality close to 16-bit LoRA. The trade-offs are slower training steps because of repeated dequantization, and a subtle deployment issue: merging adapters into a dequantized base gives slightly different weights than those used in training, so outputs should be re-evaluated after merging.
u: Fine-tuning large LLMs on a single GPU
Low-budget domain adaptation experiments
Academic research on limited hardware
qlora.x: A university lab with a few 24 GB GPUs uses QLoRA to adapt a 30B-class open model to clinical note summarization. Running the base in 4-bit lets each experiment fit on one card, and they evaluate the merged model separately before deployment to confirm quality matches the adapter-on-quantized setup.

adapters.d:
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or PEFT, is a family of methods that adapt a pretrained model to a new task by training only a small number of added or selected parameters while the original weights stay frozen. Bottleneck adapters, the original approach, insert small modules inside each Transformer layer: a down-projection to a low dimension, a nonlinearity and an up-projection, added back through a residual connection.

Other PEFT methods include LoRA, which adds low-rank updates to weight matrices; prefix and prompt tuning, which learn virtual tokens; and IA³ and BitFit, which train scaling vectors or only biases. The shared benefits are lower training memory, tiny per-task checkpoints, and one base model that switches behavior by loading different adapters. Classic adapters add sequential computation at inference, which increases latency slightly, whereas LoRA can be merged into the weights. PEFT methods generally match full fine-tuning on moderate tasks but may fall short when the task differs greatly from pretraining.
adapters.f: h ← h + W_up·σ(W_down·h),  W_down ∈ ℝ^(m×d), m ≪ d
u: Multi-task models with per-task adapter modules
Cheap fine-tuning under limited GPU memory
Storing many customer-specific model variants
adapters.x: A translation provider keeps one multilingual base model and trains a small adapter per language pair and domain. Adapters are loaded on demand for each request, so adding a new domain means training and storing a few megabytes instead of copying the full model.
adapters.c:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class BottleneckAdapter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, bottleneck=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.down = nn.Linear(d_model, bottleneck)
        self.up = nn.Linear(bottleneck, d_model)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.up.weight)        # start as identity mapping
        nn.init.zeros_(self.up.bias)

    def forward(self, h):
        return h + self.up(torch.relu(self.down(h)))   # residual adapter

layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model=512, nhead=8, batch_first=True)
for p in layer.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False                   # freeze the pretrained layer
adapter = BottleneckAdapter(512)

x = torch.randn(4, 20, 512)
y = adapter(layer(x))                         # only adapter params get gradients
trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in adapter.parameters())
frozen = sum(p.numel() for p in layer.parameters())
print(trainable, frozen)

prompttuning.d:
Prompt tuning and prefix tuning adapt a frozen language model by learning continuous vectors that act like extra tokens, instead of changing the model's weights. Prompt tuning prepends a small number of trainable embeddings, often 20 to 100 virtual tokens, to the input embedding sequence only. Prefix tuning instead learns key and value vectors prepended at every attention layer, giving it more influence over the computation.

Only these soft prompt parameters are trained, so each task needs a few thousand to a few hundred thousand parameters, and a single batch can mix requests for different tasks by attaching different prompts. Prompt tuning was shown to approach full fine-tuning quality as model size grows into the billions of parameters, but it is noticeably weaker on smaller models and harder tasks. Training can also be unstable and sensitive to initialization; initializing virtual tokens from embeddings of real words related to the task usually helps. Soft prompts are not human-readable text.
prompttuning.f: input = [P₁, …, P_m ; E(x₁), …, E(x_T)],  only P trained
u: Lightweight per-task adaptation of frozen LLMs
Mixed-task batching on one shared model
Multi-tenant serving with tiny task parameters
prompttuning.x: A platform team offering classification tasks to many internal groups trains a soft prompt for each task on a shared frozen model. Because requests differ only in their prepended vectors, the server can batch tasks together, though for their smaller models they found LoRA gave better accuracy on harder tasks.
